I am a 58-year-old woman who has farmed in Quzhou County my whole life, and my education has taught me to read the extension bulletins and trust the science from the agricultural station here. My family has five mu of flat, irrigated land. At the start of this growing season, my winter wheat is already in the ground from last October—it is greening up now after the cold months. I will manage it through spring with top-dressing nitrogen at green-up and jointing, irrigate at the critical jointing, heading, and grain-filling stages, and spray for weeds, aphids, and fusarium head blight. I expect a good yield because I planted an improved semi-dwarf variety. After harvest in early June, I will immediately plant hybrid summer maize using no-tillage seeding directly into the wheat stubble to save moisture and time. I will fertilize the corn based on the county recommendation of roughly 16 kg nitrogen per mu, applied in two splits, and irrigate at the jointing-big trumpet and grain-filling stages. I stick to this wheat-maize double cropping because it is the most reliable way to feed my family and earn cash from the grain buyer, and at my age I do not want the back-breaking labor and market risk of vegetables. My neighbor tried spring peanuts last year and the price dropped, so I will not deviate from what works.
